metadata.title: THE ROLE OF SUBNATIONAL GOVERNMENTS IN ADULT SKILLS SYSTEMS: IRELAND

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD country note is a descriptive governance overview of Ireland’s adult skills system and does not analyze student microdata from an ILSA/NAEP/PISA-type assessment. As a result, there is no sampling frame, no plausible-value (PV) scaling, and no survey-weighting or replicate-weighting procedure to document for student achievement outcomes. The tables present governance responsibilities and expenditure shares at subnational levels rather than model-based estimates from a complex survey. For this type of policy mapping, analysts would not use ILSA weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) because no ILSA micro-dataset is used.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the document does not conduct any student-level assessment scoring or modeling of cognitive achievement outcomes from an ILSA/NAEP/PISA-type test. Instead, it summarizes institutional responsibilities and governance structures for adult skills policy in Ireland using administrative/policy information. Missing-data handling is not reported because there is no statistical estimation procedure on microdata (no imputation/deletion strategy is needed for a qualitative/policy description).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Not applicable: the note is a policy governance country description and does not define an analytic student sample from an assessment dataset.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Ireland country note describes how adult skills systems are governed across national, regional, and local levels, and how responsibilities and funding are allocated across policy areas (VET, HVET, CET, adult education, and ALMPs). It reports a governance structure (combined model) and provides tables mapping which level is responsible for strategy, intelligence, implementation, funding, and delivery for each policy area. The note also lists key institutions (e.g., SOLAS, ETBs, Quality and Qualifications Ireland, Department of Social Protection/Intreo, Regional Skills Fora, and local authorities) and explains their roles in aligning provision with regional and local labour market needs. Because it is not an empirical student-assessment analysis, it does not use assessment instruments, plausible values, sampling weights, or ML models, and therefore provides no predictive performance metrics or benchmark effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse because the document is a descriptive OECD country note rather than an empirical large-scale assessment study. It does not analyze student-level assessment data, does not estimate statistical models, and does not report ML algorithms, PV handling, missing-data procedures, or sample sizes. Consequently, fields related to ILSA-based predictive modeling (main_findings, confounders, ML techniques, and sample composition) are intentionally left empty.
